images.title: Which mat is larger?
images.purpose: Show that laying mat P and mat Q on each other does not settle which is larger, because neither fits inside the other, and that counting equal squares does: 14 and 16.
images.composition: On the left the two mats laid on each other, on the right the same mats counted in unit squares.
images.exact_structure: Plain white frame, 1456 by 816. At the top, centred at x 728 and y 62, the heading Which mat is larger? in dark #1F2937 bold sans-serif (44 px). LEFT panel, two mats laid on each other: mat P is a rectangle of 7 by 2 unit squares, 280 by 80 px, at x 120 to 400 and y 340 to 420, filled teal #0072B2 with a thin dark #2B2B2B outline (3 px) and no inner lines; mat Q is a square of 4 by 4 unit squares, 160 by 160 px, at x 180 to 340 and y 300 to 460, drawn on top as an outline only with an amber #E69F00 line (8 px) and no fill, so Q sticks out above and below P and P sticks out to the left and to the right of Q. RIGHT panel, the same two mats on a grid of 40 px squares, side by side: mat P at x 780 to 1060 and y 240 to 320 made of 14 unit squares in 2 rows of 7, filled teal with thin dark grid lines (2 px); mat Q at x 780 to 940 and y 400 to 560 made of 16 unit squares in 4 rows of 4, filled amber with thin dark grid lines (2 px). Under the left panel, centred at x 260 and y 540, the caption Lay one on the other; to the right of mat P, centred at x 1180 and y 285, the caption 14 squares; to the right of mat Q, centred at x 1180 and y 480, the caption 16 squares; above mat P, centred at x 920 and y 210, the caption Mat P; above mat Q, centred at x 860 and y 370, the caption Mat Q; all in dark #1F2937 bold (36 px). In all 2 mats in each panel, 14 and 16 unit squares. No other number and no other text anywhere. Nothing else in the frame.

images.takeaway: When neither shape fits inside the other, cover both with the same small square and count: the mat with more squares has the larger area.
images.description: Mat P of 7 by 2 squares and mat Q of 4 by 4 squares laid on each other with neither covering the other, and the same mats counted: 14 and 16 squares.
images.context: Concept image for Comparing Areas: Which Is Larger?. It follows the idea of rectangles A, B and C in your maths book (shapes laid on each other, then counted on a grid) and uses the numbers of this concept's own example.
images.teaching_notes: Let the student see where Q sticks out and where P sticks out before they count. The slip to watch: deciding by the longer side only.

image_decisions.why: The two panels show why laying one shape on the other can fail and why equal squares work.
